name: Cardiogen

card.summary: An Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg tetrapeptide from Khavinson's lab aimed at heart tissue; sparse rat and cell data, no human trials.
card.note: Research peptide; extremely thin evidence base.

quick.overview:
Cardiogen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as acting on cardiovascular tissue.

The literature is thin: cell and rat experiments only, and no human studies. It has no documented appearance use.
quick.mechanism: Reported to stimulate proliferation in heart-tissue cultures and lower the pro-apoptotic protein p53, and to interact with DNA and histones [1].
quick.risks: In a rat transplanted-sarcoma model it was reported to inhibit tumour growth [2]; no human safety data exist, and it is not an approved medicine.

lead: Cardiogen is a synthetic tetrapeptide, Ala-Glu-Asp-Arg (AEDR), of about 489 daltons, developed in the research program of Russian gerontologist Vladimir Khavinson at the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and described as a cardiovascular-targeted bioregulator [1][3]. It is discussed within the wider anti-aging peptide field, where people interested in healthy ageing and a younger-looking body follow the Khavinson bioregulators [3].

Reported work is limited to organotypic cultures, cell lines and rats, including stimulation of proliferation in heart tissue explants from young and old animals, reduced p53 expression, and dose-dependent inhibition of transplanted M-1 sarcoma growth in senescent rats [1][2]. Reports of smaller heart-attack damage in rats come from a patent and are not directly confirmed by peer-reviewed literature, according to the Grokipedia summary [1]. Cardiogen is not approved for human therapeutic use and is sold as a research chemical [1].
infobox: Not approved for human therapeutic use [1]

paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946 to 2024) directed the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and promoted peptide bioregulators as geroprotectors; Wikipedia lists organ-derived preparations such as Thymalin and Epithalamin approved in Russia and the CIS, along with shorter synthetic peptides, though its article does not mention Cardiogen [3]. Wikipedia notes that its account relies largely on his own publications and carries a promotional-content banner [3].

An AI-generated encyclopedia summary reports that Cardiogen increased proliferation in rat heart explants from young and old animals, reduced p53, raised cytoskeletal proteins 2 to 5 times in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, and binds DNA and histones [1]. In senescent rats with transplanted M-1 sarcoma, Cardiogen injections raised tumour-cell apoptosis and inhibited tumour growth in a dose-dependent manner via haemorrhagic necrosis and apoptosis, according to the study abstract [2]. The same summary links the peptide to senescence-related cardiac impairment as a hypothesis [1].
No regulatory approval and no registered human clinical trials exist, according to the Grokipedia summary, and suppliers sell it as a research chemical disclaiming human use [1].
No studies found. Laboratory and rat research is described above [1][2].

timeline.event: Study reports Cardiogen effects on M-1 sarcoma in senescent rats [2].

refs.title: Tumor-modifying effect of cardiogen peptide on M-1 sarcoma in senescent rats

chain: Proposed to counter age-related decline in cardiac cells
angle.text: Cardiogen is framed within a gerontology program as a heart-tissue regulator that may counter cell senescence. People who follow anti-aging peptides pursue it for longevity and vitality; no cosmetic use is described in the published material.
